podcast.body: Released in the fall of 1970, this song directly challenged the South's history of racism and slavery, with lyrics urging listeners to "not forget about your Bible or your good book." The song provoked anger among many white southerners who felt it broadly condemned the entire white population of the South. Years later, in his 2012 biography, Young reflected on the song, admitting that he disliked his own words, finding them "accusatory and condescending." "Southern man released in the fall of nineteen seventy. This song was upsetting to many white southerners."

podcast.body: Released in 1970, this song directly called out the American South for its racism, history of slavery, and the use of religion (specifically the Bible, referred to as "your good book") as a justification for these practices. The lyrics included "Don't forget what your good book says / Southern change gonna come at last / Now your Southern man / Will you know when freedom comes? / Well I heard screaming and the whole world is clapping and I don't know." The song was highly upsetting to many white people in the South, who felt it painted them in broad, racist strokes. Years later, Young himself reflected on the song in his biography, stating he deserved to be called out for it. "Young called out the South for its racism its history of slavery and he also calls out their use of religion. The Bible and religion was used as a justification for slavery and he uses it here in Southern man he says don't forget about your Bible he specifically adds your when he says your good book which of course is the Bible."

Neil Young later acknowledged that "Southern Man" was "simplistic and condescending." "Neil Young even said he was honored to be name checked in the Leonard Skinnerd hit."
